pr_body:
It's possible for a zombie process to have live threads. These are not listed
in /sys in "cgroup.procs" but they show up in "tasks" nodes. When killing a
cgroup, let's kill threads instead of processes, so the live threads of a
zombie get killed too.

Closes #12262.
pr_comments:
This looks incorrect. Killing the thread group leader should bring the whole process down. We should not go and kill individual threads, that's just gonna break stuff. apps should know better how to bring their threads down if we want to kill them, hence we should only kill the thread group leader and the rest will follow automatically.

Also, this patch doesn't work on cgroupsv2. There, the "tasks" file is gone entirely, since it never made sense to expose cgroups per-thread...

And no, to my knowledge if a thread group leader dies the thread group goes away wholly. So this doesn't make semantical sense to me at all I must say

The problem is that the thread group leader is a zombie while other threads are alive. If "tasks" will not available in the future, what would you suggest instead?

This makes a difference as the shutdown is clean again, so something must be better than before. As we're going to kill everything in the cgroup anyway, I don't think killing some threads earlier than others should break any services.
Whoops, I looked at wrong (parent) "cgroup.procs", the process is actually listed. You're right, let's scratch this.

Actually I was probably looking at `/sys/fs/cgroup/systemd/user.slice/user-1000.slice/user\@1000.service/dbus.service/cgroup.procs` (which includes the PID) instead of `/sys/fs/cgroup/unified/user.slice/user-1000.slice/user\@1000.service/dbus.service/cgroup.procs`, which is indeed empty. How can they be different?

> It's possible for a zombie process to have live threads.

I was only able to recreate this by calling `syscall(SYS_exit, 0)` directly as recent glibc uses exit_group(2). But lets assume this somehow happens.

Signal is delivered to arbitrary thread but if it is a fatal signal, all threads in the threadgroup are forcefully terminated.

Sending a signal to PID of the whole process should be thus enough. @topimiettinen What kernel version/release is this?

@Werkov Debian Buster 4.19.0-5-amd64.

The problem is not killing the process, but noticing first that it exists. Cgroup v2 "cgroup.procs" does not list zombies.

Chiming in from cgroup v2 side, I agree with @poettering in saying that I'm not convinced this makes sense. If the thread group leader is AWOL and gone zombified, that's something that any init can't really hope to sensibly deal with. This may "fix" this bug, but I'm worried it will cause an indefinite slow grind of undebuggable new ones, since applications no longer control thread lifetime.

This seems to be a bug in kernel and it may be fixed one day, so then this change for systemd would not be needed. The question for systemd is how new kernels we require and how critical we see this bug. For most participants this seems to be in heisenbug / minor annoyance category, so perhaps it's not worth changing systemd after all.

Yeah, if the process iterator mistakenly skips zombies with live threads (which it seems it does), that's a kernel bug. I'm just not convinced we should try to do anything about it in systemd. It seems TJ is already aware of the issue.

Hmm, patch looks OK if this is what it takes to fix things on old kernels. But at least there should be a comment about this, plus a hint when this got fixed in the kernels. Also, can we find a way to not require the "triple" killing spree on kernels that don't need it?

It should be possible to cut this down to "double" killing at least, by checking cg_unified_controller(SYSTEMD_CGROUP_CONTROLLER) first, no?

Does this bug actually apply to both cgroupv1 and cgroupv2 equally?

/cc @htejun

The bug is only present in v2:
```
28767 pts/0    Zl     0:00 [zombie-thread2] <defunct>
$ grep 28767 /sys/fs/cgroup/unified/user.slice/user-1000.slice/session-1.scope/cgroup.procs 
$ grep 28767 /sys/fs/cgroup/systemd/user.slice/user-1000.slice/session-1.scope/cgroup.procs 
28767

cgroup2 on /sys/fs/cgroup/unified type cgroup2 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime,nsdelegate)
cgroup on /sys/fs/cgroup/systemd type cgroup (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime,xattr,name=systemd)
```
So the extra killing spree could be avoided on v1. Also, there's no need ever to use v1 "threads".  

After having killed all processes, the number of surviving zombie threads to be killed should be very low (typically there are none) and thus there should not be too much wasted effort anyway.

FTR, @htejun already prepared a [fix](https://www.spinics.net/lists/cgroups/msg22387.html) in the listing of such processes.

Also, when I consider it now, I'm not convinced a process (not task/thread) with live threads is a true zombie. The current behavior is to send SIGCHILD to the parent only when the last thread of the process terminates. All in all, do we need any (temporary) fix in systemd?

@Werkov It's something in between. Anyway, the fix for the kernel bug is in 5.2-rc5 (c03cd7738a83). With a fixed kernel (or cgroupsv1) the zombies are reported correctly. The commit adds support for older kernels with cgroupsv2. I'd expect that downstreams either fix their kernels, or use this a patch like this to avoid doing that. Alternatively systemd upstream can also include the fix and it seems @poettering is agreeable to that.

> I'd expect that downstreams either fix their kernels, or use this a
> patch like this to avoid doing that.
+1

> Alternatively systemd upstream can also include the fix 
-1

```A stop job is running for User Manager for UID 1000 (1min 10s / 2min)```
I tried to find out what is causing this, creating a log according to [Debugging](https://freedesktop.org/wiki/Software/systemd/Debugging/).

**Used distribution**

**Expected behaviour you didn't see**

 > Delay when shutting down

**Steps to reproduce the problem**
Shutdown the system

[shutdown-log.txt](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/files/3060571/shutdown-log2.txt)

@poettering The problem is that the zombie thread is not listed in "cgroup.procs". Not listing zombies is actually a kernel feature for cgroupv2:
> After exit, a process stays associated with the cgroup
> that it belonged to at the time of exit until it's reaped; however, a
> zombie process does not appear in "cgroup.procs" and thus can't be
> moved to another cgroup.

This can be demonstrated with the zombie-thread.c program:
```
$ ps x|grep zombie[-]
   1424 ?        Ss     0:00 ./zombie-thread
   1425 ?        Zl     0:00 [zombie-thread] <defunct>
$ grep State /proc/1425/task/*/status
/proc/1425/task/1425/status:State:      Z (zombie)
/proc/1425/task/1426/status:State:      S (sleeping)
# cgroup v2
$ grep 142[4-6] /sys/fs/cgroup/unified/user.slice/user-1000.slice/session-1.scope/cgroup.procs 
1424
$ grep 142[4-6] /sys/fs/cgroup/unified/user.slice/user-1000.slice/session-1.scope/cgroup.threads 
1424
1426
# cgroup v1
$ grep 142[4-6] /sys/fs/cgroup/systemd/user.slice/user-1000.slice/session-1.scope/cgroup.procs 
1424
1425
```
Because the zombie process is not found in "cgroup.procs", `cg_kill()` will not find it and then it won't kill the live thread, which will block the shutdown.

I think not listing zombies is a misfeature for the kernel as this makes "cgroups.procs" not fully authoritative source.

Not sure why people think it's useful to keep posting on al old bug. Summary is this: some user service doesn't want to shut down on SIGTERM when systemd --user tries to end the session. Because of that things have to time-out, and because of that systemd --user itself has to wait before it can shutdown. The system instance of systemd (i.e. systemd --system) then reports that on screen as systemd --user not shutting down.

Figure out which user service is responsible. It's almost certain systemd is just the messenger here, and not at fault itself, but some user service that just doesn't want to die and thus causes everything else to hang too and systemd decides to take action after the timeout.

Check the system logs to see what service this is, this is a logged event.

last time this has been discussed among the developers we figured a nice approach to hande this better (i.e. make it easier to track down the faulty user service), is to make systemd --user use sd_notify() status text notifications aggressively to tell systemd --system what it is doing and waiting for. and then make systemd --system to include the most recent status text of the service in its console status output. That way you'd see on screen which user service is causing all this.

It's just a matter of actually implementing this.

And no, just shortening the timeout to someting small is not a "fix". It's an invitation to data loss really. We cannot just go and kill user stuff too agressively, it's very much possible that the system is just slow, thus any default timeout must be chosen beyond the time where "system is just slow" territory is left, and the territory of "things are clearly hung" is entered. And given that that line is blurry we better go for timeouts that are too long than too short.

If you read through the comments though, user experience is in a big part in this. And that can't be fixed by "just fixing the various root causes", as there are various daemons and things causing this issue. This is issue will pop up time and time again.

Give users a way to kill the process forcefully if something is taking too long. It's up to them to judge the situation based on what is hanging, and with the changes you were talking about for showing which user service it is, users will have the information they need to know if they want to kill a process or not.

If you hit C-A-D more than 7 times within 2s the system will instantly reboot, and not wait for offending services. It will still try to sync file systems and so on, but hanging services won't cause further delays. It's the escape hatch if shutdown is hung and you don' want t wait anymore. It's not a hard power off, and not a clean shutdown, but something reasonably in the middle.

C-A-D 7 times to kill everything is not reasonable compared to just killing that one specific service that is hanging. It's an obscure way of killing (compared to say ctrl+c), and on top it does too much in comparison. Just let users force kill the one hanging service.
I am sorry, but during system shutdown there's no UI running. We can only use the most basic if input events the kernel provides us with, C-A-D handling.

Would you at least consider giving users more hints in the message that we all googled for and ended up here?
E.g. when my system all of a sudden hung for 2min I **didn't know** that I could hit C-A-D 7 times and obviously there's no way to open a browser at that point and search.

Similarly, I've tried to search logs for this event but there's a ton of output and I don't know what exact string I'm searching for, I didn't notice it. not sure i follow? i mean there are two kinds of signals in a way:

1. SIGKILL + SIGSTOP which are kernel operations on tasks pretty much, which cannot be caught, blocked or ignored. They execute a kernel operation on a task, and userspace cannot  interfere, see signal(7) about that.

2. All the others are mostly just friendly requests to the app: the app can catch them, can block them, can ignore them. The kernel only operates on them if the app doesn't handle them themselves.

This means that there's no need to deliver SIGTERM, SIGHUP and friends to all threads/zombie threads or so of a process, because they are just friendly anyway, and if a process is in such a weird state it's not going to react to friendly requests anyway. OTOH SIGKILL/SIGSTOP is something we need to rely on, because that is supposed to really make evreything go away. Hence as I understand it should matter to deliver SIGKILL (and maybe SIGSTOP) to all those weird threads, but for the other kind of signals we don't have to and probably really shouldn't.

Do I make any sense?
